L11: L12: Navigation L13: L14: For skill creators L15: L16: Using scripts in skills L17: L18: For skill creators L19: # Using scripts in skills L20: L21: How to run commands and bundle executable scripts in your skills. L22: L23: Copy page Copy page L24: L25: Skills can instruct agents to run shell commands and bundle reusable scripts in a `scripts/` directory. This guide covers one-off commands, self-contained scripts with their own dependencies, and how to design script interfaces for agentic use. L26: ## L27: L28: cite3†​ L29: L30: One-off commands L31: L32: When an existing package already does what you need, you can reference it directly in your `SKILL.md` instructions without a `scripts/` directory. Many ecosystems provide tools that auto-resolve dependencies at runtime. L33: L34: * uvx L35: L36: * pipx L37: L38: * npx L39: L40: * bunx L41: L42: * deno run L43: L44: * go run L45: L46: cite4†uvx†docs.astral.sh runs Python packages in isolated environments with aggressive caching. It ships with cite5†uv†docs.astral.sh . L47: L48: `uvx ruff@0.8.0 check . L49: uvx black@24.10.0 . L50: ` L51: * Not bundled with Python — requires a separate install. L52: * Fast. Caches aggressively so repeat runs are near-instant. L53: L54: cite6†pipx†pipx.pypa.io runs Python packages in isolated environments. Available via OS package managers (`apt install pipx`, `brew install pipx`). L55: L56: `pipx run 'black==24.10.0' . L57: pipx run 'ruff==0.8.0' check . L58: ` L59: * Not bundled with Python — requires a separate install. L60: * A mature alternative to `uvx`. While `uvx` has become the standard recommendation, `pipx` remains a reliable option with broader OS package manager availability. L61: L62: cite7†npx†docs.npmjs.com runs npm packages, downloading them on demand. It ships with npm (which ships with Node.js). L63: L64: `npx eslint@9 --fix . L65: npx create-vite@6 my-app L66: ` L67: * Bundled with Node.js — no extra install needed. L68: * Downloads the package, runs it, and caches it for future use. L69: * Pin versions with `npx package@version` for reproducibility. L70: L71: cite8†bunx†bun.sh is Bun’s equivalent of `npx`. It ships with cite9†Bun†bun.sh . L72: L73: `bunx eslint@9 --fix . L74: bunx create-vite@6 my-app L75: ` L76: L77: * Drop-in replacement for `npx` in Bun-based environments. L78: * Only appropriate when the user’s environment has Bun rather than Node.js. L79: cite10†deno run†docs.deno.com runs scripts directly from URLs or specifiers. It ships with cite11†Deno†deno.com . L80: L81: `deno run npm:create-vite@6 my-app L82: deno run --allow-read npm:eslint@9 -- --fix . L83: ` L84: L85: * Permission flags (`--allow-read`, etc.) are required for filesystem/network access. L86: * Use `--` to separate Deno flags from the tool’s own flags. L87: cite12†go run†pkg.go.dev compiles and runs Go packages directly. It is built into the `go` command. L88: L89: `go run golang.org/x/tools/cmd/goimports@v0.28.0 . L90: go run github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/cmd/golangci-lint@v1.62.0 run L91: ` L92: L93: * Built into Go — no extra tooling needed. L94: * Pin versions or use `@latest` to make the command explicit. L95: L96: Tips for one-off commands in skills: L97: * Pin versions (e.g., `npx eslint@9.0.0`) so the command behaves the same over time. L98: * State prerequisites in your `SKILL.md` (e.g., “Requires Node.js 18+”) rather than assuming the agent’s environment has them. For runtime-level requirements, use the cite13†`compatibility` frontmatter field . L99: * Move complex commands into scripts. A one-off command works well when you’re invoking a tool with a few flags. When a command grows complex enough that it’s hard to get right on the first try, a tested script in `scripts/` is more reliable. L100: ## L101: L102: cite14†​ L103: L104: Referencing scripts from `SKILL.md` L105: L106: Use relative paths from the skill directory root to reference bundled files. The agent resolves these paths automatically — no absolute paths needed. List available scripts in your `SKILL.md` so the agent knows they exist: L107: L108: SKILL.md L109: L110: `## Available scripts L111: L112: - **`scripts/validate.sh`** — Validates configuration files L113: - **`scripts/process.py`** — Processes input data L114: ` L115: L116: Then instruct the agent to run them: L117: SKILL.md L118: L119: `## Workflow L120: L121: 1. Run the validation script: L122: ```bash L123: bash scripts/validate.sh "$INPUT_FILE" L124: ``` L125: L126: 2. Process the results: L127: ```bash L128: python3 scripts/process.py --input results.json L129: ``` L130: ` L131: L132: The same relative-path convention works in support files like `references/*.md` — script execution paths (in code blocks) are relative to the skill directory root, because the agent runs commands from there. L133: ## L134: L135: cite15†​ L136: L137: Self-contained scripts L138: L139: When you need reusable logic, bundle a script in `scripts/` that declares its own dependencies inline. The agent can run the script with a single command — no separate manifest file or install step required. Several languages support inline dependency declarations: L140: L141: * Python L142: L143: * Deno L144: L145: * Bun L146: L147: * Ruby L148: L149: cite16†PEP 723†peps.python.org defines a standard format for inline script metadata. Declare dependencies in a TOML block inside `# ///` markers: L150: scripts/extract.py L151: L152: `# /// script L153: # dependencies = [ L154: # "beautifulsoup4", L155: # ] L156: # /// L157: L158: from bs4 import BeautifulSoup L159: L160: html = '

Welcome

This is a test.

' L161: print(BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser").select_one("p.info").get_text()) L162: ` L163: L164: Run with cite5†uv†docs.astral.sh (recommended): L165: L166: `uv run scripts/extract.py L167: ` L168: `uv run` creates an isolated environment, installs the declared dependencies, and runs the script. cite6†pipx†pipx.pypa.io (`pipx run scripts/extract.py`) also supports PEP 723. L169: L170: * Pin versions with cite17†PEP 508†peps.python.org specifiers: `"beautifulsoup4>=4.12,<5"`. L171: * Use `requires-python` to constrain the Python version. L172: * Use `uv lock --script` to create a lockfile for full reproducibility. L173: L174: Deno’s `npm:` and `jsr:` import specifiers make every script self-contained by default: L175: scripts/extract.ts L176: L177: `#!/usr/bin/env -S deno run L178: L179: import * as cheerio from "npm:cheerio@1.0.0"; L180: L181: const html = `

Welcome

This is a test.

`; L182: const $ = cheerio.load(html); L183: console.log($("p.info").text()); L184: ` L185: L186: `deno run scripts/extract.ts L187: ` L188: * Use `npm:` for npm packages, `jsr:` for Deno-native packages. L189: * Version specifiers follow semver: `@1.0.0` (exact), `@^1.0.0` (compatible). L190: * Dependencies are cached globally. Use `--reload` to force re-fetch. L191: * Packages with native addons (node-gyp) may not work — packages that ship pre-built binaries work best. L192: L193: Bun auto-installs missing packages at runtime when no `node_modules` directory is found. Pin versions directly in the import path: L194: scripts/extract.ts L195: L196: `#!/usr/bin/env bun L197: L198: import * as cheerio from "cheerio@1.0.0"; L199: L200: const html = `

Welcome

This is a test.

`; L201: const $ = cheerio.load(html); L202: console.log($("p.info").text()); L203: ` L204: L205: `bun run scripts/extract.ts L206: ` L207: * No `package.json` or `node_modules` needed. TypeScript works natively. L208: * Packages are cached globally. First run downloads; subsequent runs are near-instant. L209: * If a `node_modules` directory exists anywhere up the directory tree, auto-install is disabled and Bun falls back to standard Node.js resolution. L210: L211: Bundler ships with Ruby since 2.6. Use `bundler/inline` to declare gems directly in the script: L212: scripts/extract.rb L213: L214: `require 'bundler/inline' L215: L216: gemfile do L217: source 'https://rubygems.org' L218: gem 'nokogiri' L219: end L220: L221: html = '

Welcome

This is a test.

' L222: doc = Nokogiri::HTML(html) L223: puts doc.at_css('p.info').text L224: ` L225: L226: `ruby scripts/extract.rb L227: ` L228: * Pin versions explicitly (`gem 'nokogiri', '~> 1.16'`) — there is no lockfile. L229: * An existing `Gemfile` or `BUNDLE_GEMFILE` env var in the working directory can interfere. L230: ## L231: L232: cite18†​ L233: L234: Designing scripts for agentic use L235: L236: When an agent runs your script, it reads stdout and stderr to decide what to do next. A few design choices make scripts dramatically easier for agents to use. L237: ### L238: L239: cite19†​ L240: L241: Avoid interactive prompts L242: This is a hard requirement of the agent execution environment. Agents operate in non-interactive shells — they cannot respond to TTY prompts, password dialogs, or confirmation menus. A script that blocks on interactive input will hang indefinitely. Accept all input via command-line flags, environment variables, or stdin: L243: L244: `# Bad: hangs waiting for input L245: $ python scripts/deploy.py L246: Target environment: _ L247: L248: # Good: clear error with guidance L249: $ python scripts/deploy.py L250: Error: --env is required. Options: development, staging, production. L251: Usage: python scripts/deploy.py --env staging --tag v1.2.3 L252: ` L253: ### L254: L255: cite20†​ L256: L257: Document usage with `--help` L258: `--help` output is the primary way an agent learns your script’s interface. Include a brief description, available flags, and usage examples: L259: L260: `Usage: scripts/process.py [OPTIONS] INPUT_FILE L261: L262: Process input data and produce a summary report. L263: L264: Options: L265: --format FORMAT Output format: json, csv, table (default: json) L266: --output FILE Write output to FILE instead of stdout L267: --verbose Print progress to stderr L268: L269: Examples: L270: scripts/process.py data.csv L271: scripts/process.py --format csv --output report.csv data.csv L272: ` L273: Keep it concise — the output enters the agent’s context window alongside everything else it’s working with. L274: ### L275: L276: cite21†​ L277: L278: Write helpful error messages L279: L280: When an agent gets an error, the message directly shapes its next attempt. An opaque “Error: invalid input” wastes a turn. Instead, say what went wrong, what was expected, and what to try: L281: L282: `Error: --format must be one of: json, csv, table. L283: Received: "xml" L284: ` L285: ### L286: L287: cite22†​ L288: L289: Use structured output L290: L291: Prefer structured formats — JSON, CSV, TSV — over free-form text. Structured formats can be consumed by both the agent and standard tools (`jq`, `cut`, `awk`), making your script composable in pipelines. L292: L293: `# Whitespace-aligned — hard to parse programmatically L294: NAME STATUS CREATED L295: my-service running 2025-01-15 L296: L297: # Delimited — unambiguous field boundaries L298: {"name": "my-service", "status": "running", "created": "2025-01-15"} L299: ` L300: Separate data from diagnostics: send structured data to stdout and progress messages, warnings, and other diagnostics to stderr. This lets the agent capture clean, parseable output while still having access to diagnostic information when needed. L301: ### L302: L303: cite23†​ L304: L305: Further considerations L306: * Idempotency. Agents may retry commands. “Create if not exists” is safer than “create and fail on duplicate.” L307: * Input constraints. Reject ambiguous input with a clear error rather than guessing. Use enums and closed sets where possible. L308: * Dry-run support. For destructive or stateful operations, a `--dry-run` flag lets the agent preview what will happen. L309: * Meaningful exit codes. Use distinct exit codes for different failure types (not found, invalid arguments, auth failure) and document them in your `--help` output so the agent knows what each code means. L310: * Safe defaults. Consider whether destructive operations should require explicit confirmation flags (`--confirm`, `--force`) or other safeguards appropriate to the risk level. L311: * Predictable output size. Many agent harnesses automatically truncate tool output beyond a threshold (e.g., 10-30K characters), potentially losing critical information. If your script might produce large output, default to a summary or a reasonable limit, and support flags like `--offset` so the agent can request more information when needed. L312: Alternatively, if output is large and not amenable to pagination, require agents to pass an `--output` flag that specifies either an output file or `-` to explicitly opt in to stdout.
